justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modestly upward-drifting baseline from what I'd assume is a current price near 302–303, likely for an equity index, commodity, or similar financial instrument. For the one-day horizon, I anchored close to the last observed level with only a small upward nudge, reflecting the general tendency of risk assets to drift slightly higher on any given day when no strong directional catalyst is present. For the one-week estimate, I extended that drift marginally further, acknowledging that a week provides enough time for incremental positive momentum to compound while still being too short for major fundamental repricing. The one-month estimate steps up a bit more, consistent with a long-run expected return assumption of roughly 8–10% annualized translated into a monthly increment, while remaining conservative enough to reflect mean-reversion tendencies if the asset has recently outperformed.

The confidence interval widths were calibrated primarily by realized and implied volatility at each horizon, with uncertainty scaling roughly with the square root of time — a standard feature of random-walk-like price processes. At one day, the interval is relatively tight because most of the noise that could move prices dramatically (overnight gaps, surprise announcements) has a low base rate on any particular day. By one week, the range widens to reflect accumulated daily moves and the higher probability of a macro event, earnings release, or geopolitical development occurring within that window. By one month, the interval is nearly four times as wide as the daily one on each side, reflecting genuine uncertainty about where the asset will be trading after four or five weeks of compounding randomness and potential regime changes.

Specific risks that could push outcomes outside my stated intervals include a surprise central bank policy shift — an emergency rate move or unexpectedly hawkish forward guidance — which historically can produce single-session moves of 3–5% or more, easily breaching the one-day bounds. On the upside, a strong macro surprise such as a blowout employment report, a geopolitical resolution, or a major stimulus announcement could push prices well above the upper bound of even the monthly interval. Liquidity events, such as a flash crash or a large forced seller, could also temporarily breach the lower bound without any fundamental news driving it.

Finally, I should note that my intervals implicitly assume roughly normal or slightly fat-tailed return distributions. In practice, financial returns exhibit heavier tails than a normal distribution implies, meaning true tail events — a market dislocation, a sovereign default scare, or a pandemic-style shock — are more likely than my stated 90% confidence interval formally acknowledges.
